item.title: The Locked-Out Generation: Why First-Time Homebuyers Keep Getting Older
item.body:
For decades, buying a first home was a milestone people expected to reach in their twenties or early thirties. That expectation has shifted. According to recent annual surveys from the National Association of Realtors, the median age of first-time buyers has climbed to roughly 38, up from about 29 in the early 1980s. The share of first-time buyers among all purchasers has also hovered near record lows. Exact figures vary by year and survey, but the direction is clear: the entry point to homeownership keeps moving later in life.

## Why the Door Is Harder to Open

Three forces work together to delay purchases.

### 1. High prices

Home prices rose sharply during the pandemic years and have mostly held their gains since. Incomes have grown too, but not as fast as prices in many metro areas. The result is a wider gap between what a typical household earns and what a typical home costs. A larger down payment, even a modest one of 5% to 10%, now takes years of saving, especially for renters who also face rising living costs.

### 2. Elevated mortgage rates

Mortgage rates were below 3% for a stretch in 2020 and 2021. Since then they have been far higher. A higher rate raises the monthly payment on the same loan, which cuts the price a buyer can afford. Even a gap of one or two percentage points can add hundreds of dollars to a monthly payment and shrink a buyer's budget by tens of thousands of dollars.

### 3. Thin inventory

Many current homeowners hold low-rate mortgages from earlier years. Selling would mean trading that loan for a much more expensive one, so many choose to stay put. This "lock-in effect" keeps fewer existing homes on the market. At the same time, years of underbuilding, along with zoning limits and higher construction costs, have left a shortfall in entry-level housing. With fewer choices, buyers compete for the same modest homes, which supports prices.

## What Delay Means for Families

The timing of homeownership is tied closely to other life decisions.

- **Family plans.** Surveys regularly find that housing costs are one reason some adults postpone having children or have fewer than they wanted. A stable home, space for a growing family and a good school district often figure into these choices.
- **Where people live.** Some buyers move to lower-cost regions or accept longer commutes. Others stay with parents or share housing longer than they would like.
- **Career flexibility.** Renters can move easily, but they also face rent increases and less control over where they live. Buyers who stretch to purchase may feel less able to change jobs or cities.

None of this is a rule for every household, and many people are happy renting. But for those who want to buy, the delay carries real costs.

## The Wealth-Building Gap

Housing is the largest asset for many American families. Homeowners build equity as they pay down a mortgage and, in most periods, as home values rise. Buying at 38 instead of 28 means ten fewer years of that process.

Federal Reserve data consistently show that homeowners have a much higher median net worth than renters. Part of that gap reflects age and income, since homeowners tend to be older and earn more. Still, a later start leaves less time to build equity before retirement, and it can mean carrying a mortgage into later years.

There is also a generational question. Older cohorts often bought when homes were cheaper compared with incomes. Younger adults who start later may find it harder to match their parents' wealth, and may have less to pass on or less ability to help their own children.

## The Wider Housing Market

An older first-time buyer affects more than one household.

- **Slower move-up chain.** Starter homes are the first link. When fewer first-time buyers enter, owners of those homes have fewer buyers, which can slow the sequence of sales that frees up larger homes.
- **Rental demand.** Households that stay renters longer compete for apartments and single-family rentals, which can keep rents elevated.
- **Local economies.** Home purchases support spending on furniture, repairs and services. Fewer and later purchases can soften those effects.

## What Could Help

No single fix exists, and economists disagree about the best mix. Commonly discussed approaches include:

- **Building more homes**, particularly smaller and lower-priced ones, by easing zoning and permitting limits.
- **Down payment assistance** programs offered by states and localities, which can help qualified buyers close the savings gap. These can also add demand, so their effect on prices is debated.
- **Falling mortgage rates**, which would improve affordability but could also bring more buyers and more competition.
- **Easing the lock-in effect**, through ideas such as portable or assumable mortgages, though each has trade-offs.

## What Prospective Buyers Can Do

Individual choices cannot solve a market-wide problem, but some steps may help:

1. Check your credit report and work on your score before applying.
2. Set a realistic monthly budget that includes taxes, insurance and maintenance, not only the mortgage payment.
3. Look into state and local assistance programs and first-time buyer loan options.
4. Compare lenders, since offers can differ meaningfully.
5. Consider a wider search area or a smaller property as a first step.
6. Keep an emergency fund so that buying does not leave you without a cushion.

## The Bottom Line

The rising age of the typical first-time buyer reflects a housing market where prices, borrowing costs and limited supply all push in the same direction. The delay shapes when families form, how quickly households build wealth and how the market functions. Easing it will likely take a mix of more construction, better access to credit and time.

*This article is for general information only and is not financial, legal or investment advice. Statistics cited are approximate and may change; consult current data from sources such as the National Association of Realtors, the Federal Reserve and Freddie Mac, and speak with a qualified professional before making housing decisions.*
